bib.title: MAPLE: A Sub-Agent Architecture for Memory, Learning, and Personalization in Agentic AI Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MAPLE: A Sub-Agent Architecture for Memory, Learning, and Personalization in Agentic AI Systems", Deepak Babu Piskala, arXiv 2602.13258v1 (3 Feb 2026). Submitted to the ALA 2026 workshop at AAMAS 2026, so a workshop submission, not a peer-reviewed result. Code: github.com/prdeepakbabu/maple-framework (not read).

COVERAGE: 51573 of 51573 chars read (all pages, references, Appendix A). The extraction is clean. Figures were checked by caption only, not viewed.

FIT WARNING: Poor to moderate fit for 03b. It is a user-personalization architecture paper, not agent learning from task experience. Its only experiment compares a stateless baseline with the full system, using synthetic personas and an LLM judge. It has no raw-vs-distilled ablation, no memory-maintenance experiment, no cost or latency comparison, and no full-context baseline. The "distilled vs raw" and "transfer" ideas appear only as design argument plus one transfer-flavoured test. Use it as a light citation (a design taxonomy plus a weak with/without-memory number), not as evidence for a ranking of memory designs.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Claim: MAPLE beats a stateless baseline on judge-scored personalization.
 number: 4.17 to 4.78 (+0.61), "14.6% relative"; Welch t=6.05, df 74.5, Cohen's d=0.95
 setup: 150 synthetic personas, 10-turn dialogues generated by Claude 3 Haiku. Turns 1-8 are the learning phase and turns 9-10 are the evaluation phase. Generator is Claude 3 Sonnet; judge is Claude 3 Haiku on a 5-point scale. Single run, no seeds or intervals given. The df of 74.5 does not match n=150 personas (or 300 turns), and the paper does not explain the unit of analysis.
 quote: "The mean personalization score improves from 4.17 to 4.78, representing a 14.6% relative gain. We assess statistical significance using Welch's t-test for unequal variances, obtaining t= 6.05 with 74.5 degrees of freedom and p< 0.001."
 where: Sec 6.4, p8, Table 1
2. Claim: Learned traits show up in answers to unrelated test queries (transfer to novel topics), and the baseline shows them far less.
 number: trait incorporation 45% to 75% (+30pp); perfect 5/5 scores 15% to 88%
 setup: same as claim 1. Test queries are "deliberately unrelated to previously discussed topics". The traits are mostly user attributes (diet, kids, pets), not task skills.
 quote: "The Trait Incorporation Rate rises from 45% to 75%, a 30 percentage point absolute improvement." and "the proportion of responses receiving perfect personalization scores (5/5) increases from 15% to 88%"
 where: Sec 6.4, p8
 caveat: the baseline gets only the current turn's query and no history, yet it still shows 45% incorporation and a 4.17 mean. The judge scores a 3 for "generic but helpful", so the scale is compressed near the top. A baseline "trait incorporation" of 45% with zero memory also suggests the judge is lenient or that traits are guessable from the query; the paper does not address this.
3. Claim: Learning (extraction) should run asynchronously, outside the request path. This is a design assertion with no latency experiment behind it.
 number: Memory plus Personalization add "15-70ms latency"; Learning takes "minutes to hours"
 setup: stated for the authors' reference implementation, which uses deterministic database queries. No measurement table.
 quote: "Memory and Personalization operate in the request path (adding 15-70ms latency through deterministic database queries), while Learning operates in the background (minutes to hours)"
 where: Sec 4.1, p5
4. Claim: Raw episodic records and distilled semantic records should both be kept. Episodic is the material for learning; semantic is the efficient input for personalization. This is an argument, not a measured result.
 number: none
 quote: "episodic captures what happened; semantic captures what we've concluded. Systems need both. Episodic provides material for Learning; semantic provides efficient input for Personalization."
 where: Sec 3.1.1, p3-4
 related: a three-level hierarchy (raw interactions, session summaries, user models, cohort patterns) is cited to HippoRAG [5]; recursive summarization [27] is cited for compression.
5. Claim: Learning is "symbolic" (stored in external structures, not weights). This avoids catastrophic forgetting across users and keeps preferences editable. This is also design reasoning, not a test.
 number: none
 quote: "(1) No catastrophic forgetting—insights about Sarah don't overwrite knowledge about Marcus, since they reside in separate database entries rather than shared parameters; (2) Immediate editability"
 where: Sec 3.1.1, p4
6. Claim: Three levels of learning: replay of trajectories, strategy extraction, skill synthesis. Replay is "brittle otherwise" when situations differ. Untested.
 number: none
 quote: "Level 1—Replay: Store successful trajectories, retrieve by similarity... This is case-based reasoning [25]—powerful when situations match, brittle otherwise."
 where: Sec 3.1.3, p4
7. Claim: Memory maintenance appears only as context-rot risks plus claimed mitigations (selective retrieval, hierarchical compression, conflict resolution preferring recent explicit feedback over old implicit signals). No implementation or evaluation is reported for these. Stale or wrong memories compound.
 number: none
 quote: "If Sarah's preference was incorrectly recorded, every subsequent interaction reinforces that error." and "prioritizing recent explicit feedback over old implicit signals"
 where: Sec 5, p6. Event-triggered updates for thumbs-down feedback are in Sec 3.1.4.
8. Claim (a design fact, not a result): the reference Memory is a plain filesystem of JSON, with no vector DB and no embeddings. The authors claim the gains come from the M/L/P decomposition, not from retrieval quality.
 number: none (three directories: users/, episodic/, semantic/)
 quote: "no vector databases, no embedding models—shows that personalization gains come from the M/L/P decomposition, not from retrieval optimization."
 where: Sec 4.2, p5
 caveat: the experiment never compares decomposed against monolithic memory, so this claim is not supported by the data.
9. Claim: Context budget illustration: user-preference memory takes 15% of the window. Illustrative, not measured.
 quote: "system prompts (10%), conversation history (20%), tool declarations (10%), user preferences from memory (15%), the current query (5%), and unused context for reasoning (40%)"
 where: Fig 4 caption, p6

BASELINES
- Only one baseline: a stateless Claude 3 Sonnet that sees the current turn only.
- There is no full-context baseline (the whole 8-turn history in the prompt). That is the obvious competitor and it is absent. There is no raw-memory baseline, no RAG or vector-memory baseline, and no monolithic-memory ablation. The paper calls the study an "ablation" but it only removes everything.
- Not compute or token matched. MAPLE adds LLM calls (the Learning sub-agent runs on each turn, with its own LLM instance) plus injected context. Token cost, dollars and Learning-call counts are not reported. The only cost number is the 15-70ms retrieval latency.
- The judge is given the revealed trait list, so the grading is aligned with exactly what MAPLE extracts. The paper concedes possible self-preference bias, since both generator and judge are Claude. Its mitigation (Sonnet generator, Haiku judge) is weak. It states that there is no human evaluation.

LIMITS (conceded and observed)
- Conceded: synthetic personas and LLM-as-judge; self-preference bias; three sub-agents need coordination infrastructure; personalization quality is subjective; cross-user learning needs anonymization. Future work: human evaluation, other judges (GPT-4, Llama), federated learning with differential privacy, longitudinal production deployment.
- Observed: a single 10-turn horizon, so there is no long-term maintenance, drift or contradiction test. Traits are simple static facts (diet, pets), so they tell us little about learning procedural knowledge or strategies. The Level 2 and 3 learning is never run. The "p<0.01" in the abstract and "p<0.001" in the text differ. The stated "14.6%" is 0.61/4.17, which is correct. The Sarah and Marcus examples are hypothetical, not experiments. The models are Claude 3 era and so dated. The dataset is promised on Hugging Face ("will be released"), so it was not checked.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
MemGPT (Packer 2023); Generative Agents (Park 2023); HippoRAG (Gutiérrez 2024); Recursive Summarization (Wang 2023); CoALA (Sumers 2023); Tulving 1972 and Squire 2004 (memory types); Reflexion (Shinn 2023); ReAct (Yao 2023); LaMP (Salemi 2024); PEARL (Mysore 2023); user modeling (Fischer 2001, Rich 1979); self-citations on file-based agent design (Piskala 2025, 2026, arXiv:2601.11672); LLM-as-judge (Zheng 2023); the context-rot taxonomy of poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash is cited to [11], which is Ring Attention (Liu 2024). That looks like a mis-citation.

CODE (verbatim, Appendix A.1, p10, Learning extraction prompt, abridged)
Analyze this conversation turn and extract insights about the user. ... Extract ANY useful insights about the user: - PREFERENCE ... - FACT ... - BEHAVIOR ...
Return insights as JSON array: [{"type": "preference|fact|behavior", "content": "detailed insight text", "confidence": 0.0-1.0}]
Also the user model: U_u = (S_u, D_u, B_u, G_u), meaning static, dynamic, behavioral and predictive (Eq. 1, Sec 3.2.2). The closed loop is M -retrieves-> P -adapts-> r -feedback-> L -writes-> M (Eq. 2).

FIGURE candidate: Figure 3 (p4), "MAPLE architecture as a sequence diagram showing the request-time flow (steps 1-4) and background learning loop (steps 5-6)". It shows the split between the request path and the asynchronous learning path faster than prose. Figure 4 (p6, context budget percentages) is illustrative only, with no measurement. Figure 5 (p8) is just the Table 1 bars.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction is clean, but the equations and the closed-loop arrows are garbled in places. Citation [11] looks wrong (see BUILDS ON). The abstract says p<0.01 while the text says p<0.001. The df of 74.5 is inconsistent with n=150 and is unexplained. The dataset and code were not checked.
